title: light passed hand to hand
hook: fire that couldn't burn a blade of grass, and why Hindus offer a flame back to God

segments.voice: Yesterday: namaste, I bow to you, and the bow that touches an elder's feet. Today, the flame that comes around on a plate.

Evening at a temple, or a living room when the lamp comes out. A small flame sits on a metal plate, and someone moves it in slow circles before the shrine. A bell rings. People sing. Then the plate is carried around the room, and one by one, people pass their hands over the flame and bring their palms to their eyes and forehead. Why offer fire to God at all? An old story has an answer.
screen: `A FLAME ON A PLATE.` → `SLOW CIRCLES. A BELL.` → `WHY OFFER FIRE TO GOD?`

segments.voice: Arti: the waving of a lamp, the offering of light. The best-known song begins om jai jagadish hare: victory to you, lord of the world. Now the story, from one of the oldest Hindu texts. The gods once won a great victory and grew proud: we did this. Then a strange being appeared before them, and nobody knew who it was. They sent Agni, the god of fire. I can burn anything on earth, he boasted. The being set down a single blade of grass. Burn this. Agni rushed at it with everything he had, and couldn't burn it. The god of the wind went next: I can blow away anything. He couldn't move the grass. Then Indra, king of the gods, came near, and the being vanished. In its place stood a shining goddess, Uma, who told him: that was Brahman. The victory was Brahman's all along. Fire burns because of Brahman, not on its own. Another old line says it: everything shines after that one shining, even this little fire. Many teachers read arti this way: a small flame is light offered back to where light comes from. Then it leaves the shrine and goes to the people, and each person draws its warmth to their eyes: the same fire for every face. Often prasad follows: food offered to God, handed back as a blessing. Whatever shines in you, a gift, a good day, a win, the old answer is the same. It's borrowed light. Offer it back, then share it.
screen: `ARTI — THE OFFERING OF LIGHT` · `FIRE COULDN'T BURN ONE BLADE OF GRASS` · `EVERYTHING SHINES AFTER THAT ONE` · `THE SAME FIRE TOUCHES EVERY FACE`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. If there's a candle or a lamp near you, look at it; any light in the room will do. Cup your hands toward it, as if gathering warmth, and bring them to your eyes and forehead. Then bring one person to mind and turn your cupped hands toward them, as if passing the plate.
Arti. The offering of light, and then the light shared with everyone. Fifth word.
Your line: light passed hand to hand. Next time the plate comes around, you'll know what you're doing. Day five.

howItsDone: Arti is performed in temples and homes, often in the morning and evening: a lamp is waved before the image of God while a bell rings and a song is sung, and then the flame is brought to each person, who passes their hands over it and touches their eyes and forehead.

story.title: the blade of grass
story.text: After a great victory, the gods grow proud. A mysterious being appears. Agni, the fire god, boasts he can burn anything; he can't burn the single blade of grass it sets before him. The wind god can't move it. When Indra comes near, the being vanishes, and the goddess Uma tells him it was Brahman, whose victory it had been all along.
